paras: The Hickory church burning was a night attack at Hickory, Mississippi, in which a Black church was fired into and burned and the town calaboose was burned, around the turn of 1881–82. Three white men and a Black man were arrested on the charges, and a judge went to the town to investigate. The one surviving report, from the Brandon Republican, described a community stirred by lawlessness that its officials had failed to stop.

According to the Brandon Republican, the church, described only as "a negro church," was fired into and burned on "Monday night last." The calaboose at Hickory was burned the same night. The brief gave no name for the church, no motive and no report of anyone hurt.

Three white men and a Black man, none named, were arrested on charges of firing into and burning the church and burning the calaboose. Judge Mayers left for Hickory to investigate the charges. The paper wrote that "a good deal of excitement" prevailed over "the lawlessness of certain parties, and the failure of the local officials to suppress it." No report of the investigation's result, an indictment or a trial appears in the coverage.

The story survives only as a short brief from the Brandon Republican, reprinted in other Mississippi weeklies. The Pascagoula Democrat-Star ran it without a headline or credit among filler items, in an issue catalogued as December 30, 1881. The Weekly Clarion of Jackson reprinted it on January 18, 1882, under the heading "Alleged Lawlessness Near Hickory Mississippi" with credit to the Brandon Republican. Neither paper added comment, and both identified the church and the accused by race while placing the blame for disorder on local officials.

The date of the attack is uncertain because both copies count "Monday night last" from a Brandon Republican issue whose date is not given. The Democrat-Star's catalog date would place the attack in December 1881, but the same page carries a review of crime "during the year 1881" and a dispatch dated January, so that page may have been printed later.
